meta.title: Who originally recorded "Mustang Sally"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Wilson Pickett. Mack Rice wrote it and cut it first, as "Sir Mack Rice" on Blue Rock in May 1965 — an R&B hit before Pickett's 1966 Atlantic version.
meta.ogDescription: Wilson Pickett's 1966 Atlantic cut is the famous one, but Mack Rice wrote the song and recorded it first, on Blue Rock in May 1965.

answer.label: Not a Wilson Pickett original — a 1965 Sir Mack Rice single on Blue Rock
answer.originalArtistDates: 1933–2016 · American soul singer and songwriter, born in Clarksdale, Mississippi
answer.sourceLine: Ask most people who made “Mustang Sally” and you get Wilson Pickett. But the song was written and first recorded by Mack Rice, issued in May 1965 on Mercury’s soul subsidiary Blue Rock under the billing “Sir Mack Rice.” Rice’s own record was no obscurity — it reached No. 15 on the U.S. R&B chart. Pickett cut it for Atlantic in 1966, and that version became so definitive that the 1965 original effectively vanished from public memory.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Blue Rock
original.released: Issued as a 7-inch single, Blue Rock 4014, in May 1965, credited to “Sir Mack Rice”, with “Daddy’s Home to Stay” on the B-side. Blue Rock was Mercury Records’ Chicago-based soul subsidiary, active 1964–1969.
original.charted: Reached No. 15 on the U.S. R&B chart in 1965 — a genuine hit, not a flop that needed rescuing.
original.cover: Wilson Pickett recorded it for Atlantic Records in 1966, released on the album The Wicked Pickett. It reached No. 6 R&B, No. 23 pop, No. 4 in Canada and No. 28 in the UK (No. 62 on 1987 reissue), and was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2000.
trail: The Wikipedia article on the song ↗ states plainly that Mack Rice wrote and first recorded it, released on Blue Rock in May 1965 as “Sir Mack Rice”, and that his version reached No. 15 R&B.
MusicBrainz ↗ holds the Sir Mack Rice recording at 3:06, attached to the 1965 US single paired with “Daddy’s Home to Stay”.
Blue Rock Records ↗ is documented as a Mercury soul subsidiary running 1964–1969, and lists Mack Rice’s 1965 “Mustang Sally” among its releases.
Rice’s biography ↗ confirms he sang with the Falcons from 1957 to 1963 alongside Wilson Pickett — the two men knew each other long before the cover.

authors.name: Sir Mack Rice
authors.heading: Sir Mack Rice
authors.metaLine: 1933–2016 · Detroit soul singer · Blue Rock Records, 1965
authors.bio: Bonny “Mack” Rice was born in Clarksdale, Mississippi in 1933 and moved to Detroit in 1950, where he sang with the Falcons from 1957 to 1963 alongside Eddie Floyd and a young Wilson Pickett. He wrote “Mustang Sally” and cut it himself for Blue Rock in May 1965, billed as “Sir Mack Rice”; it climbed to No. 15 on the R&B chart. As a performer he charted only twice — the other was “Coal Man” in 1969 — but as a writer he was formidable, co-writing “Respect Yourself” with Luther Ingram for the Staple Singers. He died in the Detroit area in 2016.

authors.name: Wilson Pickett
authors.heading: Wilson Pickett
authors.bio: Wilson Pickett, born in Prattville, Alabama in 1941, was one of soul music’s defining voices, with more than fifty charting R&B records and a Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction in 1991. He and Mack Rice had sung together in the Falcons before either went solo. His 1966 Atlantic recording of “Mustang Sally”, from the album The Wicked Pickett, reached No. 6 R&B and No. 23 pop and was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2000. Nothing about the record is a mistake — it is simply not the first one.

misattribution.heading: The record, corrected
misattribution.intro: “Mustang Sally” is one of the most-covered songs in soul, and the version everyone carries in their head is Wilson Pickett’s. It is a cover.

items.why: His 1966 Atlantic recording is the standard reference version — a Grammy Hall of Fame inductee and a bar-band staple — so it is routinely treated as the song’s first appearance.

items.who: Sir Mack Rice, Blue Rock 4014, May 1965
items.why: Rice cut the song himself and it reached No. 15 on the U.S. R&B chart in 1965, the year before Pickett recorded it.
Rice wrote the song outright — here the first recording artist and the songwriter are the same person, which is what makes the misattribution unusually complete.

misattribution.truthLine: Wilson Pickett made it famous in 1966. Mack Rice wrote it and recorded it first, in 1965.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: Mack Rice’s version was not a failure that Pickett rescued. It was an R&B hit in its own right, peaking at No. 15 in 1965 on Blue Rock, a Mercury soul subsidiary based in Chicago that ran from 1964 to 1969 and never had the reach of Atlantic. That is most of the story: the same song, a year apart, on labels with wildly different promotional muscle and pop-crossover reach.

The rest is the record itself. Pickett’s Atlantic cut crossed to No. 23 on the pop chart and No. 28 in the UK, became a bar-band and wedding-set standard, entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2000 and landed on Rolling Stone’s 500 Greatest Songs list. An R&B chart entry from a Mercury imprint could not survive that. There is even a wrinkle about how Pickett got it: Felix Cavaliere of the Young Rascals claimed in liner notes that Atlantic took the song from his band and handed it to Pickett.
detailsBody: Mack Rice writes the song after a visit to singer Della Reese, where her drummer and bandleader Calvin Shields says he would rather have a Ford Mustang than a Lincoln Continental.
Rice’s working title is “Mustang Mama”; Aretha Franklin suggests “Mustang Sally” instead, after the name he had already used in the chorus.
May 1965: Blue Rock 4014 is released, credited to “Sir Mack Rice”, backed with “Daddy’s Home to Stay”.
1965: the single reaches No. 15 on the U.S. R&B chart.
1966: Wilson Pickett records it for Atlantic; it appears on The Wicked Pickett and reaches No. 6 R&B, No. 23 pop, No. 4 in Canada and No. 28 in the UK.
1987: Pickett’s version is reissued in the UK and charts again at No. 62.
2000: Pickett’s Atlantic recording is inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.
context.pull: Rice’s record was a hit. Pickett’s was a monument.
